text:
All three use the same design: one `createBoxOffice` closure that hides the hold and order records, ID counters, expiry and pricing behind the five-method `BoxOffice` interface. That shared structure is deep, so the scores differ only in how the internal helpers split up the work.

**A** (`A/src/boxOffice.ts`): `orderTotalCents` hides the discount and the Rappen rounding behind a two-argument call. `taken(matches, now)` hides the "active hold or non-cancelled order" rule behind a predicate, and `getOpenHold` hides the lookup plus the `UNKNOWN_HOLD` rule. However, the current time is passed into `taken` and `availableAt` as a parameter, so every caller has to deal with time. `confirm` and `release` each repeat the `now() >= expiresAt` check themselves, so expiry knowledge is spread out instead of kept in one place.

**B** (`B/src/boxOffice.ts`): `takenTickets(belongs)` reads the clock and applies all the "what counts as taken" logic itself, so callers only supply a predicate. `openHold` returns `{hold, expired}`, which handles lookup, ended-state checking and expiry in one call; `confirm` and `release` become a few lines each. `totalCents` hides the pricing rules, and `hold` reuses `available`. These helpers are the deepest of the three.

**C** (`C/src/boxOffice.ts`): `isActive` keeps expiry knowledge in one place and is reused by `ticketsWhere`, `confirm` and `release`, which is good. `unendedHold` and `totalCents` also hide their logic well. But `takenIn` and `ticketsOf` are one-line pass-throughs to `ticketsWhere`, which adds interface without hiding anything. The `{hold, ended}` wrapper shape also has to be repeated in several type annotations, so a representation detail leaks into helper signatures.

```json
{"scores": {"A": 6, "B": 7, "C": 6}}
```
